source_analysis_in_original_words: Prehistoric short a was fronted to æ except in the nasal environment described by Fulk. Later a was restored before following w, or in an open syllable when a back vowel followed in the next syllable.
The historical interplay explains the familiar nominal æ/a alternation without making a present-day mechanical spelling substitution.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Fulk’s dot over ġ is editorial; a course-style dæg is a declared removal of that dot, not an exact Fulk transcription.
Contrasts the closed syllable with dagum.

simplification_limits: Do not call the basic historical change a→ea; æ precedes breaking.
Do not apply a-restoration through an arbitrary consonant cluster; Fulk explicitly contrasts closed syllables.
The long ǣ/ā alternation is less regular (§29 p.19) and need not be added as an equally general rule.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Prehistoric front vowels acquired a following glide in particular consonantal environments: æ→ea, e→eo and i→io. In West Saxon io later becomes eo.

The main environments are h, r plus a following consonant other than j, and certain l-plus-consonant sequences. Before l+C the treatment differs by vowel: æ normally breaks, e does so regularly only before lh, and good evidence for i before lh is lacking.
Some long vowels also break before h; a short-vowel account is a bounded introduction, not an assertion that long breaking never occurred.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Asterisk is present on Fulk’s prehistoric input, not on the Old English result.
Infinitive, preterite singular, preterite plural, past/passive participle. No e-breaking in helpan before lp.
Fulk prints the input with an asterisk.

simplification_limits: Do not state that every front vowel breaks before every l+C cluster.
Breaking is historically conditioned; its examples do not license changing every manuscript e or æ in a matching-looking modern string.
Fulk Appendix A notes that alleged short-vowel breaking before w can instead be analysed as back mutation; omit a categorical w rule.

source_analysis_in_original_words: A following i or j, usually in the next syllable, caused anticipatory fronting or raising of the root vowel; the conditioning sound often later disappeared.
Useful correspondences include u/ū→y/ȳ, o/ō→e/ē, ā→ǣ, æ→e and fronting/raising of the relevant diphthongs. A broad table must distinguish the later historical stage from older e-raising.

Present second and third singulars had i-bearing endings, explaining why a mutated vowel can be restricted to those cells. Noun alternations and related weak verbs show the same type of historical conditioning.

simplification_limits: The historical conditioning i/j may be invisible in the surviving form.
Noun endings and unmutated forms can be restored by analogy (§82); umlaut is not a universal plural marker.

The compact ā→ǣ correspondence excludes the nasal-vowel history distinguished by Fulk in his table; do not turn the short list into an exhaustive context-free conversion chart.

processes.topic: Older raising versus pedagogical mutation shorthand
source_analysis_in_original_words: Germanic e was raised to i before i/j earlier than the later front-mutation process. The first component of the older back diphthong was likewise raised.
Fulk permits e→i and ēo→īe as a teaching shorthand but explicitly says that it is historically inaccurate to treat them as single later front-mutation changes.
For the familiar present-vowel alternations, explain that “mutation” in a practical paradigm groups results whose histories may differ.

exact_example_records.meaning: choose; reconstructed earlier third singular; chooses
exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Fulk rejects **ċēosiþ at the relevant earlier stage; preserve both the asterisk and editorial palatal dots in an exact source record.
Fulk contrasts the Anglian form with West Saxon hilpð; this is a dialect comparison, not two interchangeable forms added to a single required paradigm.

simplification_limits: Cook §17 already warns that e→i is not strictly umlaut. Do not invent a disagreement where Cook supplies the same caution.
Do not give the equation ēo→īe as a complete single-stage historical derivation.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Strong-verb principal parts preserve inherited vowel alternations. Later regular sound changes reshape the older series, so superficially different subclasses can share an inherited pattern.
Ablaut is distinct from a vowel assimilating to an i/j in the next syllable. The Old English learner encounters it as a lexical principal-part system.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: The four columns are infinitive, preterite singular, preterite plural and participle; they are not a single time-ordered sound-change chain.
Source uses band; preserve the course’s separately evidenced spelling choices if its selected form differs.

simplification_limits: An arrow drīfan→drāf→drifon would wrongly suggest sequential historical derivation; use a slash or labelled columns.
Do not imply all strong classes have one identical OE vowel formula or that weak verbs have no historical vowel alternations.
Detailed PIE accent and zero-grade reconstruction is beyond a short appendix; Fulk Appendix A VI supplies further reading.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Certain back-of-mouth consonants shifted toward the hard palate in contact with historical front sounds. Different consonants and positions had different conditions.
Later changes can put a front vowel beside a consonant that had remained velar. Therefore modern-looking letter context alone cannot recover every historical pronunciation.
Fulk’s overdot on c/g is an editorial pronunciation distinction, not a separate Old English letter.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Course style may omit dots only by declared normalization.
Fulk contrasts the earlier front environment behind ċīest with *kōljan behind cēlan; the current front vowel alone is insufficient.

simplification_limits: Fulk says the detailed environments are not universally agreed; use a bounded practical explanation instead of pretending a short spelling rule is exhaustive.
Palatalization of a consonant and diphthongization of its neighbouring vowel are distinct changes.
The detailed sc exceptions and reversed affrication need at most a source note in this appendix.

source_analysis_in_original_words: In West Saxon, initial palatal consonants could diphthongize following front vowels: æ/ǣ gives ea/ēa and e/ē gives ie/īe.
This followed breaking; a vowel already changed by breaking did not simply undergo this same conversion.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Exact source spelling keeps the editorial dot; proposed course display is separately recorded.
Exact dotted source spellings; not all spellings need become new course entries.

simplification_limits: This is a West Saxon-centred pattern; Fulk notes its absence in Mercian/Kentish and partial Northumbrian parallels.
Not every ea/eo/ie spelling has this origin. Do not merge this with breaking or back mutation.

source_analysis_in_original_words: A back vowel in the following syllable could induce a glide in preceding i or e. West Saxon generally shows eo because older io merged with eo.
The West Saxon change is restricted chiefly to a single intervening labial or liquid consonant; it is broader in other dialects.
Analogy frequently restores an unmutated vowel, so even a soundly stated historical rule does not predict every written variant.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: Both are exact source spellings; Fulk explicitly uses their coexistence to illustrate analogy.

simplification_limits: Do not state that any following a/u changes any preceding e into eo: in West Saxon a does not affect e, although it affects i.
Do not ignore the single-consonant condition or dialect labels.
The frequent name u/a-umlaut is not a licence to equate this process with front mutation.

processes.topic: West Germanic gemination and later j-loss
source_analysis_in_original_words: A following j commonly lengthened the preceding consonant after a light syllable; r is an important exception.
The trigger was later lost after heavy syllables, including syllables made heavy by gemination. Its effects can remain after it disappears.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: bidjan is an explicitly labelled Gothic comparandum, not an OE variant.
The r exception and preserved j, written i, make this a useful contrast.
Heavy syllable prevents the simple gemination rule; dot in sēċan is Fulk’s editorial marking.

simplification_limits: Do not explain every doubled OE consonant as j-gemination; Fulk also discusses later r/l-induced gemination.
A modern dictionary double letter is not evidence that its historical trigger is still present.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Apocope names loss at the end of a word; syncope names loss in an unstressed internal syllable.

High-vowel loss depends strongly on syllable weight. A short vowel or short diphthong before a single consonant yields the light pattern; a long vowel/diphthong or an appropriate consonant cluster yields the heavy pattern.
Analogy can restore full stems, and the detailed internal-vowel conditions are more restrictive than “delete every middle vowel”.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: The contrast is retained plural -u after the light syllable versus loss after a heavy syllable; Fulk’s palatal dot is editorial.
Course headword has its own checked vowel notation; do not silently treat that as exact Fulk spelling.
Fulk identifies hēafodes as analogical restoration of the nominative stem.

simplification_limits: Only §137a–b is relied on here; its subsection c continues beyond the inspected page.
Do not replace the actual course paradigms by a newly generalized deletion algorithm.

processes.topic: Loss of medial h, contraction and compensatory lengthening
source_analysis_in_original_words: Late prehistoric medial h was lost between voiced sounds after a stressed vowel. Where a consonant preceded h, the preceding vowel could lengthen in compensation.
Where h stood between vowels, its loss brought vowels together; contraction then removed the second vowel and left a long first vowel or diphthong.
An h before a voiceless ending was in a different environment and could remain.

simplification_limits: Contraction is not a single rule creating all forms of a contracted verb; older changes and retained h/g/w may distinguish its principal parts.
Fulk explicitly cautions that not every cell of the noun tables on p.100 is attested; do not promote the full table as corpus attestation.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Late West Saxon smoothing and Anglian smoothing are distinct developments, although both replace some diphthongs with single vowels.
LWS smoothing affects ea/ēa before c/g/h or after initial palatals, and is far from consistently represented in writing.
Anglian smoothing affects a wider set of diphthongs before velars, sometimes with r/l intervening; further vowel adjustments follow.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: The same written outcome can belong to distinct labelled temporal/dialect contexts; do not collapse the analyses.
Anglian comparison only, not an alternative required West Saxon paradigm.

simplification_limits: Never use an unlabelled universal rule “diphthongs became simple vowels”.
A short appendix can give one contrast plus a warning and leave the detailed inventories to source notes.

source_analysis_in_original_words: Some strong principal parts preserve an inherited consonant alternation from an earlier accent-conditioned voicing process. Later z→r and voiced dental→d changes reshape its results.
These older alternations differ from ordinary Old English contextual voicing of f/s/þ between voiced sounds.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: The s/r contrast is inherited and does not mean that s is pronounced r in ordinary OE.
Historical dental alternation, not a licence to interchange written ð and d.

simplification_limits: Do not use present-day OE stress to derive the alternation: Fulk places the process before the Germanic accent shift.
Not every g/h contrast is Verner’s law; final devoicing also operates (§§64,85).

source_analysis_in_original_words: An older nasal before certain voiceless fricatives was lost, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel. This helps connect otherwise surprising cognates.

exact_example_records.limits_or_normalization: fimf is explicitly a Gothic comparandum, not an OE word.
Preserve Fulk thorn in the source record; course mūð involves an explicitly declared thorn/eth substitution. The German comparison is not an OE glossary entry.

simplification_limits: This is a bounded older historical pattern, not a rule deleting every OE n before a fricative.

cook_reconciliation.finding: Cook gives a→ea regularly and e/i→eo frequently, then explicitly corrects its own a shorthand to historical æ. Fulk supplies more exact vowel-specific l+C restrictions. Use Fulk for the historical rule; this does not require labelling Cook’s qualified account an error.

cook_reconciliation.finding: Cook already says i is not strictly umlaut of e immediately after helpan/hilpð. Fulk agrees and explains the older initial raising behind ēo→īe. Preserve the distinction between practical mutation labels and a multi-stage historical account.

recommended_scope: Prioritize mechanisms and familiar alternations: historical notation; ablaut versus umlaut; brightening/restoration; breaking; i-umlaut and older raising; palatal effects; back mutation; vowel loss/contraction. Add gemination, consonant alternation and smoothing as compact explanatory notes. Avoid an exhaustive PIE reconstruction course.
normalization_policy: Keep exact source strings in the evidence. If main prose uses course spelling, individually declare removal of Fulk’s editorial palatal dots, any thorn/eth substitution and any change from Fulk vowel spelling. A starred preform remains starred; a form from another language remains labelled.
unresolved_for_coordinator: Choose final examples and verify their course/glossary routes in the design audit; this source audit gives headword relationships, not a declaration of glossary completion.

If the appendix uses a reconstructed i-bearing ancestor of fēt, obtain the exact reconstruction separately: §82 directly attests the OE paradigm and identifies mutation but does not print a complete fōt derivation.
Do not derive an unattested intermediate solely by applying the compact rules unless the contract explicitly labels a source-supported rule formation.
not_assigned: No Fulk exercise, reading passage or full new paradigm is assigned. No required-recall milestone is created.
